walkthrough: The text appears before its backdrop. `BackdropFade` then builds a rounded plate from the text bounds, adding padding to give the label breathing room.
The plate’s opacity controls contrast against the scene, and persist keeps it after the animation finishes. This is useful when several items should read as one card.
experiments: Change the horizontal and vertical padding independently and inspect the spacing around the text.
Set persist to false and compare what remains after playback.

walkthrough: The rectangle and label form one `VGroup`, so the blink affects the entire recording badge. The introduction happens first, followed by three blinks over 1800 milliseconds.
Blinking changes opacity, giving attention without moving the object. Compare the badge with the stationary heading to see the effect clearly.
experiments: Keep duration fixed and double blinks to increase the pulse frequency.
Apply Blink only to the label to compare a blinking word with a blinking badge.

walkthrough: A circle and its PING label appear together, then two `BoundaryRipple` animations use the circle as their boundary reference.
Each ripple expands an outlined boundary and fades it outward. The different expandScale and strokeWidth values let you compare the size and weight of the two pings.
experiments: Increase expandScale while keeping duration fixed and inspect the larger reach.
Use the nodeGroup as the target instead of the circle and compare its measured boundary.

walkthrough: The completion card arrives before either flash. `FlashFinish` first uses white, then repeats with a green accent and a slightly stronger intensity.
The short flash sits on the same target group rather than relocating it. It can emphasize a landing or completion while the original card stays readable afterward.
experiments: Lengthen the flash from 250 to 800 milliseconds and compare how it changes the sense of impact.
Reduce intensity and inspect whether the text remains easier to read during the flash.

walkthrough: A button-shaped group is introduced, then receives two `PopHighlight` animations. The first peaks at scaleFactor 1.22 and the second at 1.35.
The effect enlarges the button and settles it back, letting a size change suggest selection without choosing a new permanent size.
experiments: Compare the two scaleFactor values at the same duration.
Apply the highlight to the label alone to see how grouping changes the effect.

walkthrough: The orb and its label form the target of `PulseGlow`. Two pulses change the aura behind that group over 1200 milliseconds.
Color, opacity and padding describe the aura’s appearance separately from the orb’s own fill. A gentle pulse can draw attention while keeping the subject stationary.
experiments: Increase padding and compare the glow’s reach around the orb.
Increase pulses with the same duration to make the breathing rhythm quicker.

walkthrough: The medal group is revealed before its celebratory particles. Two `SparkleBurst` calls compare a five-sparkle yellow burst with a four-sparkle green burst.
Count and sparkleSize control different aspects of the accent: the number of marks and each mark’s visual weight. The badge remains the stable point of attention.
experiments: Use the same sparkleSize for both bursts and compare only the count.
Choose a subtler color and smaller marks for a quieter confirmation effect.

walkthrough: The warning card first receives three angular wiggles with angle 0.14, then four smaller wiggles with angle 0.08. These angles are expressed in radians.
`WiggleHighlight` changes orientation around the target rather than making the warning text travel across the scene. Compare the larger warning with the subtler follow-up.
experiments: Hold the angle constant and vary wiggles to compare frequency.
Increase duration and watch the oscillation settle more slowly.

walkthrough: `Arrange` creates sixteen cards from one template and gives each a hue before placing them in a four-by-four grid.

The loop morphs those same cards into a radial dial, a sine curve, a line and back into a grid. Orientation and lagRatio make the transition’s direction and timing visible without replacing the cards.
experiments: Set lagRatio to zero and compare simultaneous motion with the traveling stagger.
Disable tangent orientation in the radial arrangement and inspect the card angles.

walkthrough: A five-by-five `Arrange` grid supplies one stable layout. The pattern table chooses diagonal, radial-out, snake and column ordering, pairing each with pop, fade or drop.
`Arrange.reveal` combines spatial ordering with the chosen arrival animation. The repeating loop makes it easy to compare ordering separately from styling.
experiments: Keep animation set to fade while cycling through all four patterns.
Reduce lagRatio toward zero and notice how the spatial reading order becomes less prominent.

walkthrough: The circle alternates two horizontal shifts, with `MotionPath.arc` changing the route between the endpoints. `TracePath` leaves a recent trail that exposes that route.
Both arc calls currently use height -3. The return trip reverses the displacement; the source does not change the sign of the arc height between trips. Easing controls progress along the route.
experiments: Change just the return arc’s height to +3 and compare its route.
Replace the rate function with linear while leaving the arc unchanged to separate route from pacing.
motion/arc_demo.description: A circle follows bowed routes between two endpoints. Compare the displacement direction, signed arc height and easing independently.

walkthrough: The outward trip uses one control point, producing a quadratic Bézier route. The return trip supplies two control points, producing a cubic route with a different bend.
Both trips animate position between fixed endpoints. `TracePath` records the actual movement, so you can compare the route generated by the different control-point counts.
experiments: Move the quadratic control point closer to the endpoint line and inspect the gentler bend.
Swap the two cubic control points and predict the new return route.

walkthrough: The first movement uses an X:Y frequency ratio of 1:2; the next uses 2:3. Separate amplitudes and a phase offset determine how these oscillations combine.
The circle’s trail makes the closed loops visible. These are prescribed parametric motions rather than collision-based physics.
experiments: Try equal frequencies and compare the simpler trajectory.
Change phase while keeping both frequencies fixed and inspect how the loop changes.

walkthrough: The planet begins three units from the sun and leaves a `TracePath` as it moves. A full positive turn is followed by a negative half turn.
The angle selects travel around the center, while duration and easing select the pacing. The second movement changes both direction and easing.
experiments: Keep the angle positive in both movements to compare one direction of travel.
Move the planet’s starting position farther out and inspect the larger orbit.

walkthrough: The ball travels between two endpoints at the same height. `MotionPath.parabolic` gives the outward trip height five and the return trip height three.
Linear easing keeps progress uniform while the path function supplies the arch. The trail lets you compare this planned motion with a physical projectile simulation.
experiments: Give both trips the same height and compare their routes.
Change the second endpoint’s height and inspect how the path adapts between unequal endpoints.

walkthrough: The rectangle receives a gentle shake with amplitude 0.3 and frequency 15, then a stronger one with amplitude 0.8 and frequency 25.
Decay controls how the disturbance settles. Changing amplitude, frequency and decay independently makes the difference between a small notification and a strong jolt easier to judge.
experiments: Hold amplitude fixed and vary frequency to compare quick vibration with wider-spaced movement.
Increase decay and inspect how quickly the motion settles.

walkthrough: A moving dot orbits a center marker while its radius changes. The inward trip ends at radius 0.5; the outward trip explicitly starts there and ends at radius four.
Each trip makes four turns over six seconds. The longer-lived `TracePath` records the winding shape, and easing changes how quickly the dot progresses through it.
experiments: Reduce turns to two to make individual coils easier to inspect.
Change endRadius while keeping turns fixed and compare how tightly the spiral winds.

walkthrough: The first path follows spatial waypoints, including points in front of and behind the original plane. The orbit camera helps reveal those depth changes.
The loop compares that waypoint spline with a rounded-rectangle path built by `Builder`. Both provide a route to followPath, while the sphere and trace retain their own styling.
experiments: Set all waypoint Z coordinates to zero and compare a planar route with the spatial one.
Change the rounded rectangle’s corner radius and inspect the return trajectory.

walkthrough: Three `SpringAnimation` calls compare different stiffness, damping and mass values while moving the rectangle to different targets.

The low-damping case visibly rebounds, the higher-damping case settles more gently, and the high-stiffness case gives a sharper response. These animation parameters shape motion without creating a general physics world.
experiments: Keep target and stiffness fixed while changing only damping.
Increase mass and compare the response with the lighter high-stiffness case.

walkthrough: The circle moves horizontally while `MotionPath.wave` adds a perpendicular oscillation. The outward trip uses amplitude 1.5 and four waves; the return trip uses amplitude one and six waves.
The trail separates the route from the circle’s current position. Both trips use linear easing, making the changing wave count easy to compare.
experiments: Keep amplitude fixed and compare four waves with six.
Increase duration while preserving the route to slow the same oscillating movement.

walkthrough: The infinity path first reveals its entire outline by animating the trim endpoint. A faint untrimmed copy remains behind it as a geometric guide.
The modifier then exposes one quarter of the path while offset advances through two revolutions. The source path stays fixed while its visible interval travels around the loop.
experiments: Shorten end to 0.1 during the traveling phase and compare a shorter beam.
Reverse the offset direction to make the highlighted interval travel the other way.

walkthrough: Each spoke receives `ResampleModifier` before `TwistModifier`, giving the deformation enough intermediate points to produce a smooth bend.

The custom animation raises and lowers the twist angle through a sine envelope. Radius controls the spatial extent of the twisting effect, while the shared update applies the same angle to every spoke.
experiments: Remove resampling and compare the bend of the simpler line geometry.
Reduce the twist radius and inspect how much of each spoke is affected.
